title: Agreement between subject and verb 1
subtitle: The collection houses ... / the sculptures are ...
summary: Make the verb agree with the main noun in a complex subject, with clause and what-clause subjects, with collective nouns, and with names that end in -s.

lesson.heading: The verb agrees with the main noun
lesson.text: A singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject a plural verb. When the subject is long and complex, find the **main noun** in it - that is the word the verb agrees with. This holds even when the subject comes after the verb.

examples.text: Many leading **members** of the opposition party **have criticised** the delay.
The only **excuse** that he gave for his actions **was** that he was tired.
Displayed on the board **were** the exam **results**.
examples.note: compare: The exam results were displayed on the board.

examples.text: The **collection** of seashells and fossils in the final room **is** sure to be of interest.
examples.wrong: are sure to be of interest

lesson.heading: Clause subjects
lesson.text: If the subject is a clause, we normally use a **singular** verb, however long the clause is.

examples.text: To keep these young people in prison **is** inhuman.
Having overall responsibility for the course **means** that I have a lot of meetings.

left.label: Singular main noun -> singular verb
examples: What worries us **is** the poor selection process.
What is most surprising about the building **is** the bell tower in the courtyard.

right.label: Plural main noun -> singular or plural verb
right.text: A plural verb is preferred in more formal contexts.
examples: or more colloquially: What is needed **is** additional resources.

lesson.heading: Collective nouns
lesson.text: Nouns with a singular form that refer to a group can take a singular or a plural verb. A **singular** verb focuses on the institution as one unit; a **plural** verb focuses on the individuals in it. Formal writing usually prefers the singular.

examples.text: The council **has** (or **have**) postponed a decision on the new road.
The orchestra **performs** (or **perform**) classical concerts throughout the year.
The United Nations **has** (or **have**) ordered an investigation.

lesson.note: Also: army, association, audience, class, club, college, commission, committee, community, company, crew, crowd, department, electorate, enemy, family, federation, generation, government, group, institute, jury, opposition, orchestra, population, press, public, school, team, university; the Bank of England, the BBC, IBM, Sony.

lesson.heading: When only one form will do
lesson.text: Sometimes the meaning forces the choice. If the action is something the **individuals** do, we need a plural verb; if it happens to the group as an institution or a building, we need a singular one.

examples.text: The committee usually **raise their hands** to vote 'Yes'.
examples.wrong: The committee usually raises its hands

examples.text: The **class have** all passed the end-of-year exam.
The **school is** to close next year.
examples.wrong: The school are to close next year

examples.text: The **jury includes** three adults and three children.
examples.note: include treats the group as a whole

lesson.heading: Names and titles ending in -s
lesson.text: When a name or title ending in -s refers to a **single unit** - a country, a newspaper, a book or film title, or a quoted word or phrase - we use a singular verb.

examples.text: At this time of the year the Netherlands **is** one hour ahead of the UK.
The Machine Gunners **was** one of Robert Westall's most successful books.
'Daps' **is** the word used in the south-west of the country for sports shoes.
The stairs leading to the first floor **were** steep and poorly lit.

lesson.text: Cover everything between the main noun and the verb, then read the two together: *the collection ... is*, not ~~the collection of seashells and fossils ... are~~.

exercises.prompt: The Rivers Museum on the corner of Corn Street and New Road ___ a fascinating collection of art and other objects.
exercises.explanation: The main noun is The Rivers Museum, so the verb is singular.

exercises.prompt: Among the most eye-catching pieces in the whole collection ___ the marble animal sculptures under two arches.
exercises.explanation: The subject follows the verb, and its main noun is the plural sculptures.

exercises.prompt: Whoever created these figures apparently ___ a mystery.
exercises.explanation: A clause subject takes a singular verb.

exercises.statement: The people I know who have seen the film say that it's really good.
exercises.explanation: Correct. The main noun is the plural people, so say is right.

exercises.prompt: Match each subject with the verb form it takes.

pairs.left: At this time of year the Netherlands
pairs.right: is one hour ahead of the UK.
was one of Robert Westall's most successful books.
is used in the south-west of the country for sports shoes.

pairs.left: The stairs leading to the first floor

exercises.statement: The New Straits Times report that tourism is booming in Malaysia.
exercises.explanation: The New Straits Times reports that tourism is booming in Malaysia. A newspaper title ending in -s is a single unit.

exercises.prompt: Perhaps what is most surprising about the building itself ___ the bell tower in the small courtyard.
exercises.explanation: After a what-clause subject the verb follows the main noun, and the bell tower is singular.

exercises.prompt: The Waterman's Junior Book Prize jury ___ three adults and three children.
exercises.explanation: include describes the group as a whole, so a singular verb is used.

exercises.prompt: Which verb form does each subject allow?

items.text: The school ___ to close next year.
The phrase 'men in white coats' ___ used to talk about psychiatrists.
The committee usually ___ their hands to vote 'Yes'.
The class ___ all passed the exam.
The orchestra ___ classical concerts throughout the year.
The press ___ a picture of chaos in our schools.
The university ___ to host the conference.

exercises.statement: Whoever made all the mess in the kitchen have to clear it up.
exercises.explanation: Whoever made all the mess in the kitchen has to clear it up. A clause subject takes a singular verb.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order. The subject comes after the verb here.
exercises.answer: Hanging on the wall directly opposite the carvings are over a hundred swords from the 17th century
exercises.explanation: The verb still agrees with the main noun of the subject - swords - even though the subject follows it.

exercises.statement: Over 50 full-time staff and volunteers is employed, and having so many of them available to answer questions adds to the pleasure of this must-see museum.
exercises.explanation: Over 50 full-time staff and volunteers are employed ... The subject is plural; the -ing clause that follows correctly keeps the singular adds.
